Témoin de la montée de violence dans sa: Witness to the rising violence in his hometown, Babs lived through the wars that shook Congo before finding refuge in Canada in 2019.
Babs dans la maison de son oncle à Laval: Babs at his uncle's house in Laval. Photo: Adrien Gaertner
Babs est né à Goma, la capitale de la pr: Babs was born in Goma, the capital of North Kivu province in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This region, marked by decades of armed conflict and ethnic tensions, remains to this day a hotbed of violence and brutality inflicted on civilians. We first met Babs through <l1>the demonstration organized by the Congolese community last February</l1>.
Témoin de la montée de violence dans sa: A witness to the rising violence in his hometown, the 44-year-old lived through the wars that shook Congo between 1996 and 2003 before finding refuge in Uganda, then in Canada in 2019. Listening to his testimony, we are taken back to the dawn of the thirty years of armed violence that have shaken eastern DRC.
C'est par un mercredi ensoleillé du mois: It is on a sunny Wednesday in March that we meet Babs again in Laval. Standing in front of his uncle's house, he waits for us with a proud look, hands in his pockets. His brightly patterned shirt evokes the arrival of spring.
Dans ce refuge familial où plusieurs sur: In this family refuge where several survivors have found shelter after fleeing the east of the country, we take our places in a large armchair, a symbol of his uncle's hospitality.
Goma, aujourd'hui associée à des tueries: Goma, now associated with mass killings, was not always a dangerous place. Located on the shores of Lake Kivu, the city, with its mountain climate, was once a tourist destination, Babs tells us. “It was a bit like the Bahamas,” he says, laughing.
Lorsqu’il se remémore la ville de son en: When he thinks back to the city of his childhood, what he remembers most is how close it was to Rwanda and how the border between the two countries almost disappeared. “Sometimes I would leave my house to go play in Rwanda without even realizing it. There was no border!” he exclaims. There was no physical border, and no distinction between the Congolese and Rwandan peoples, he tells us. “In primary school, I studied with Rwandans but I didn't realize they were Rwandan. It was hard to understand that we were different peoples, in different countries.” He continues: “Because we lived, played and studied together.”
« C'était une belle vie…Jusqu'à ce que l: “It was a beautiful life… Until the politicians went crazy,” he lets out.
L’année 1994 marque un tournant lorsqu’u: The year 1994 marks a turning point, when a genocide pitting Hutus against Tutsis breaks out in Rwanda. In the space of a hundred days, more than 800,000 Tutsis are killed. More than a million civilians, mainly Hutus*, flee to the DRC, fearing reprisals.
« On a vu l'arrivée en masse des réfugié: “We saw the mass arrival of Rwandan refugees. That's when life started to change,” he says.
Entre 1994 et 1996, Babs et sa famille p: Between 1994 and 1996, Babs and his family get into the habit of offering refuge to those fleeing Rwanda. “We took refugees in at our place, we let them have something to eat and a place to sleep, but some of them were very sick,” he remembers. After a pause, he catches his breath and continues: “One morning, we woke up to find that the women and children had all died in our living room. We had seen them vomiting, so we thought it was because of cholera.”
<l1>Dans son programme de communication: In <l1>its outreach programme on the genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda</l1>, the UN does indeed state that thousands of refugees were killed by waterborne diseases.
À 14 ans, Babs est alors exposé pour la: At 14, Babs is exposed to mass mortality for the first time. He goes on: “That's when I started to see the world differently. It wasn't like before. But I didn't realize that it was nothing compared to what was waiting for me,” he lets out in a deafening silence.
Parmi les réfugiés se trouvant en RDC, l: Among the refugees in the DRC, the UN notes in <l1>its outreach programme</l1> that there were also Rwandan government officials, soldiers and militiamen who had taken part in the genocide. “They came back to Congo with weapons, there was banditry, armed robberies, and that led to the creation of several armed groups,” says Babs.
Bien des années plus tard, depuis la rep: Many years later, since fighting resumed in 2021, Rwandan militias continue to carry out operations in the DRC. Their main motivation is the illegal extraction of the minerals found in Congolese soil, notably cobalt. This resource, essential in the manufacture of electronic devices, accounts for about 70% of the world's reserves found on Congolese territory, and arouses a great deal of greed.
« C'est ça la réalité du Congo. Il y a d: “That's the reality of Congo. There are dead people everywhere, all the time. And children grow up with this trauma. And it's too hard.”
D’une guerre à l’autre: From one war to the next
En 1996, le déclenchement de la guerre e: In 1996, the outbreak of war in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is largely influenced by the involvement of several regional actors, including Rwanda and Uganda. These countries consider the presence in the DRC of those responsible for the 1994 genocide, who had taken refuge there, a significant threat.
Face à cette situation préoccupante, le: Faced with this worrying situation, Rwanda and Uganda decide to intervene militarily in the DRC. In December 1996, a Rwandan operation is launched with the aim of eliminating these genocidal groups. Although this intervention succeeds in dislodging its targets, Rwandan troops remain in the DRC, altering the region's political dynamics.
Cet épisode entraîne une série d'événeme: This episode sets off a series of events, including Rwanda's support for Laurent-Désiré Kabila in overthrowing the Mobutu regime in 1997; Mobutu had been president of the DRC since 1965. These events lead to a prolonged and complex period of conflict in Congo.
Babs, résidant à Goma, est témoin de la: Babs, who lives in Goma, witnesses the rise of violence in his region: “Around May 1996, <l1>Laurent Désiré Kabila's rebels</l1> arrived in our city. Bullets were whistling, there were explosions everywhere,” he says.
Malgré la violence qui l’entoure, le jeu: Despite the violence around him, the young man remains confident about his country's future: “We had faith in our president, Mobutu. We believed he was going to act, that the situation was going to improve. But in the end, the exact opposite happened,” he continues, in a flat voice. In 1997, the Mobutu regime is overthrown by that of Laurent Désiré Kabila.
« Les militaires ont fui », poursuit -il: “The soldiers fled,” he continues. “As for us, we were just left there. We had to find a way to escape or else defend ourselves. Defending ourselves was impossible because we had no weapons,” he says with a shrug.
Babs et sa famille s’enfuient alors vers: Babs and his family then flee to a neighbouring village.
« Malheureusement, j’ai été capturé », d: “Unfortunately, I was captured,” he says quickly, as if numb to the violence he himself endured. He continues: “I was forced to join the army of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo (ADFL). I was 14, I didn't have that kind of heart.”
Durant trois mois, Babs est plongé dans: For three months, Babs is plunged into total isolation and undergoes military training that he describes as a veritable concentration camp. “I don't know if I can say it was military training or if it was torture. We barely ate. We hardly slept. We were barely clothed. And those who tried to escape, they killed them,” he lists.
Dans le salon, le temps semble s’être ar: In the living room, time seems to have stopped. The silence between Babs's words intensifies his story.
« Je devais soit me soumettre, soit mour: “I either had to submit or die,” he says. The pauses in his breathing seem endless. “There was no way out. If you left the military base, the forest was waiting for you, with its animals ready to strangle you. On the other side was Rwanda.”
Tiraillé entre la peur de s’enfuir ou de: Torn between the fear of fleeing and the fear of submitting, he makes himself a promise: “I don't want to be one of those who will traumatize others.”
« Mais j'ai quand même réussi à rentrer: “But I still managed to get back home,” he concludes, without transition. The tension in the room dissipates. He explains: “We had to go to Goma for a demonstration in front of the authorities of this movement, which is called the Passing out*. We went there on foot, covering a distance of about 40 to 50 kilometres to reach the airport.” Along the way, Babs realizes he is very close to home and runs away. “I went home. Strangely, nobody looked for me,” he concludes, a mischievous smile stretching his lips.
À peine chez lui, Babs retourne sur les: Barely home, Babs goes back to school and finishes his studies. Once he graduates at 19, the young man wants to serve his country by joining the national army. However, the rise of rebel groups quickly plunges Congo into chaos, putting Babs in danger.
Sans issue, il prend la décision de quit: With no way out, he makes the decision to leave the country and finds refuge in Uganda, where he will stay for fifteen years.
Concernant cet épisode de sa vie, Babs r: About this period of his life, Babs remains discreet. He repeats: “I can't tell you everything today.”
Après quelques secondes de silence, il l: After a few seconds of silence, he lets out: “I lost two brothers during the conflicts in the DRC. One of them was beheaded and mutilated while serving in the army fighting the M23*.” His eyes fixed on the floor, he adds: “There are so many things to share. Maybe I'll tell you his story another time.”
Alors qu’il pensait être en sécurité en: Just when he thought he was safe in Uganda, Babs realizes he is a target beyond borders. “I was threatened several times. Sometimes calls, sometimes messages. When I reported these threats to the police, they were able to trace the calls back to Rwanda,” he explains, shaking his head.
En raison de multiples menaces de mort,: Because of multiple death threats, the Ugandan government initiated an asylum request for Babs with Canada. That is how he landed in the land of the maple leaf in 2019.
« On prend mon pays pour du business ! »: “They're treating my country like a business!”
Bien que les conflits au Congo trouvent: Although the conflicts in Congo originate in the shift from the violence of the Rwandan genocide to armed clashes in eastern DRC, Babs reminds us that mining is today the main cause of the massacres that continue. “They're treating my country like a business!” he exclaims.
Depuis le début des violences armées, l': Since the start of the armed violence, the UN also estimates that the mass displacement of people within the country stands at nearly 7 million, and that more than 5 million people have died.
Bien que désormais loin du danger, Babs: Although he is now far from danger, Babs can't help following news of his country every day. “I've become Canadian, but I can't say that what's happening over there doesn't interest me. It's where I come from. Besides, I still have family there who are in danger. I have to get involved too,” he says.
Il participe régulièrement à des manifes: He regularly takes part in demonstrations organized by the Congolese community. His demands are clear: “I'm fighting so that the children in that country can know peace,” he says with dismay.
Selon les derniers chiffres de l'UNICEF: According to the latest UNICEF figures, from 2014, more than 40,000 children in the DRC work in mines.
« On ne va pas croiser les bras ! », ins: “We won't sit idly by!” he insists. “They don't even have the strength to defend themselves. Their only choice is to accept living through certain atrocities or to die,” he lets out.
« Il faut vraiment avoir un grand cœur p: “You really need a big heart to bear all this”
Aujourd’hui, Babs occupe un emploi saiso: Today, Babs holds a seasonal job with a Hydro-Québec subcontractor. Far from his native country, he speaks of rebirth. “I'm convinced that I was born into a new world here, where everything that can shock the heart, the traumatic experiences, are behind me.” He continues: “My head is calm”… before adding, with some contradiction: “I pretend to forget the past. That's what I've done.”
Malgré les défis, Babs maintient son opt: Despite the challenges, Babs maintains his optimism: “I try to keep my smile, I don't know for how long, but I think I'll manage,” he says, with a discreet smile.
Lorsque nous parlons de certaines ressou: When we bring up some mental health resources, Babs remains sceptical: “I don't need them. If I'm holding on today, it's because my brain already accepts every form of violence,” he says.
